BEHIND THE HELMET - Delivery drivers

By: Chuma Kave | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
They deliver mouthwatering food to thousands of homes daily but behind the scenes are young men and women who face constant struggles to survive and dangerous situations just to get your order on time

Unique Selling Point:
A touching case study. A driver who ran away from his war-torn country, DRC, and married a woman who also fled the war in Burundi. The film highlights his story of survival, wishes, and dreams.

The story also highlights the other disturbing trend that is taking place within the industry. The brutal daily hijackings of delivery bikes that get to be illegally shipped to places like Malawi and Mozambique.

Summary:
Food service delivery drivers, mostly belonging to Uber Eats and Mr DFood, have what some may consider an easy task - delivering mouth-watering food to thousands of homes daily. But, behind the helmet are stories of men and women who tell stories of daily struggles in what they see as a brutal industry. From app exploitation to daily muggings and hijackings, the relationship with motorists on the road, and the stories of those who are sitting home for months nursing injuries. The story follows 3 drivers.

The story ends with a sting operation in Joburg alongside a tracking and recovery company. Our cameras will follow the company as they chase the thief trying to recover another bike.

BEHIND THE HELMET - THE SCRIPT + PROMOS

UPS: Mourners “Amen” // UPS SINGING AT FUNERAL!! With subtitles..
1: At a small cemetery in Diepsloot, Johannesburg, mourners gather to pay their last respects to a fallen friend.
UPS - More singing and visuals from the funeral
2: A Burundian called Joyeux, he was just 23. A motorbike delivery rider, he was killed after colliding with a taxi.
UPS: “More singing”
3. He’s being given a dignified send-off by fellow riders who’ve raised money for his burial.
UPS: Eddy “Be confident in who you are and know that you are a child of God”
4: And if there’s an air of anxiety among those at the graveside, it’s from knowing that it could have been them being lowered into the ground.

TRANSITION TO INTRO

5..A punishing, unforgiving industry…
UPSOUND: WITNESS - This job is dangerous. I like it, but it's dangerous.
6 … a service as simple as delivering food…
JACQUES: It’s like we’re in a war
7 …becomes a constant race against the clock and… sometimes… a dice with death…

BREATHE.. PAUSE

TRANSITION TO CONTEXT SEQUENCE - DROP THE PACE A BIT
8: This is the online food delivery industry, a service that’s exploded globally in recent years and taken root in South Africa, too. Hundreds of bikers criss-cross our major cities and towns delivering restaurant fare to a hungry middle class.
PAUSE
FADE TO BLACK
LINK: “A growing army of delivery bikes are taking to the streets every day competing for scarce clients and income. But who are the men and women behind the helmets?”
VIZ.. Jacques playing with his kids
UPS: Natural sound
UPS Jacques: “Since I was born we never stayed for too long one place and were always on the run
9 Jacques - who asked us to hide his identity - fled to South Africa to escape war and poverty in the Democratic Republic of Congo.
UPS Jacques: “No time to sleep and no time to rest. No future.
10: After losing his entire family to the violence in his home country, it took Jacques five months to get here.
PAUSE
11: It’s been seven years but he says he still fears persecution as a refugee.
MAC: Why did you want to go to South Africa?
JACQUES: People were saying South Africa is safer than other countries.
12: The online food ordering platform Uber Eats had just launched in Joburg - so he signed up…renting a bike for R650 a week.
UPS: Jacques: “I start early in the morning then I knock off later around 11. Sometimes even at 12”.
VISUALS - Jacques prepares, leaves for work / Aerial shots of Cosmo City..
LINK: “Late nights, early mornings. Seven days a week. For you it is about getting your food fresh and warm and for him it is about putting food on his table…”
13: Globally, revenue in the online food delivery market is expected to reach close to a Trillion Dollars this year. More than half of that is for groceries but meal delivery is still expected to grow to close to 3 billion users in the next 4 years.
PAUSE
TRANSITION TO ESTABLISH WITNESS ON HIS OWN
UPS WITNESS: “I came here because my parents couldn’t afford to pay my school fees.
14: It’s an industry ready-made for people like Witness. Like Jacques, he fled to South Africa for a better life. Short on options as a 22-year old migrant from Zimbabwe, he found hope in an App and two wheels.
UPS WITNESS: “ When I came to South Africa I started riding a motorcycle.”
15: Witness will take work from wherever it comes… from the big names like UberEats, Mr D Food, and Bolt to smaller platforms operating in places some of the bigger brands fear to tread.
PAUSE/VISUAL SEGUE
16: But, more competition means more bikes and smaller profits.
PAUSE
UPS: Mac: Do you also rent your bike?
UPS: Witness “This one I took it on credit. I pay monthly.
Mac: You pay monthly? Yes. So this is your bike. You own it? Yes. Yes, yes. And how much are you paying monthly for this?
Witness: Yeah. This is back. I pay almost 600 every month.
WITNESS “Nowadays, it's quiet. Yeah, it's difficult to make that money. Okay, so nowadays you can make almost 3000 a week. So it's tough to budget. You are supposed to keep money for the bike. You are supposed to put in petrol. To keep money for yourself. To buy food.
17: As if his financial struggles weren’t challenging enough, Witness has also felt the brunt of another of the job’s downsides.
MONTAGE
18: This collision landed him in hospital last year and put him out of action for over a month.
UPS WITNESS: When I got injured I didn’t get paid….they said we are not employed but everyday I am going to work. I used my money to go to the hospital”
VISUALS: Witness action camera + His injury photos
UPS: FIKILE MASIKANE “They’re not doing anything to protect the drivers. They don’t have a physical place to report to”
19: Wits University Sociology Researcher Fikile Masikane is campaigning for a better deal for the gig workers in the digital economy.
UPS: FIKILE MASIKANE - “I think what we need to clarify there is that they are called partners. They're not called workers. They called themselves self-employed.”
20: For every online order, the app assigns a rider. Some days can be slow…and after expenses, profits are often slim. (PAUSE)
21: But, That isn’t their biggest concern…
LINK: “With tough bosses and demanding customers, the job is hard enough, but add rain, assault and hijackings, some drivers never make it back home..”
TRANSITION TO THE NIGHT
VIZ: Enter Rosettenville
22: As night falls, anxiety levels mount…
VIZ: Streets of Rosettenville
23: At Reaper Tactical, Roger Ladeira and his team will spend the night patrolling food franchises and recovering stolen bikes across Joburg.
We’re invited us along for the ride… bullet-proof vests… are not optional.
VIZ: Mac and recovery crew entering the cars and hitting the streets
ROGER: “From now until 9 ‘oclock it’s when the drivers are busy. This is when they do a lot of deliveries. Pizza night.
MAC: Oh yeah, it’s Friday night. Month end and it’s raining. Everybody wants to eat in. This is when all the calls start coming in.
24. For the criminals, timing is everything… striking at the end of the rider’s shifts.
ROGER: From 9 o’clock onwards that’s where they steal from the drivers houses
VISUALS: The street drive / Bikes / noise
ROGER: “What we pick up sometimes is that they make a false order, they stand outside someone’s house, wait for the driver to arrive and then attack him”
VISUALS - BIKES ON THE ROAD
LINK: “It's month-end and it’s also been raining. These guys are gonna be pretty busy tonight. The worst part about it they don’t know what they are going to encounter when they hit the roads”
25: When food orders are flowing, it’s hard to avoid hijacking hotspots.
VIZ: Mac and Roger greeting Blessing
Mac: You cover each other?
UPS: Blessing: “We cover each other or go together and make the delivery…but it's dangerous out here……we have to check what the spot is. But it's dangerous in South Hill and Bella Vista side. We cannot even avoid it because our boss said, let's work so we can work. So there's nothing you can do because we are here to work and make money. We cannot do anything”.
Visuals: More street videos
26: At a big shopping centre we run into Malik … still in shock… he’s just been assaulted.
UPS: Malik “Yeah. Just got robbed. Right now. Right now. Right now.”
27: Malik went to deliver to a customer and while waiting at their gate, a car sped up to him.
UPS: Malik “They just gave me a slap. I tried to fall down but I controlled myself. I came up, started the bike and ran away”.
Mac: Does this happen all the time
Malik: Everyday. It happens everyday.
MAC: ” How many times does it happen to you?
Malik “Maybe like seven times. Seven times? Yeah, but I'm surviving….I’m worried about my life.

28: Hijackings have escalated - the bikes chopped up for spare parts and smuggled to countries like Mozambique and Malawi.
Viz: Hijacking videos
Chopped bikes images
29: Recovery teams seldom manage to track down bikes… and suspects… before they disappear into the night…
Ups: Hijacking video
30. But sometimes, the tracking team wins: in Boksburg on Johannesbugr’s East Rand they chase down a stolen bike … after the rider is hijacked and severely pistol-whipped.
Ups: Hijacking the chase..
Mac: “Which areas would you say are some of your biggest hotspots?
ROGER: “Every area is a hotspot
MAC: “So do you think there's a big syndicate that's involved in this?
ROGER: “I do think that there is somebody that's ordering bikes”
VISUALS: MAC & ROGER on the streets
31: And, as the riders navigate the country’s treacherous criminal landscape, the fight continues with their bosses for better pay.. better support. To be “seen”.
Mac: What do you want to achieve in South Africa?
Jacques: One day I can do my own business, have my own car. Drive for Uber or Taxify. It’s safe more than these bike.

PROMOS
1 - 21 SECONDS (21 sec).
The food delivery industry in South Africa is growing rapidly but behind the scenes - it’s do …or die for the drivers.

PROMO 2 (21 sec)
An industry with so much potential but, today, being a food delivery driver in South Africa could mean signing your own death certificate!


PROMO 3 (11 sec)
We hit the streets of Rosentenville to track the lives of food delivery drivers operating at night…because for them, nothing is guaranteed…even their life.

PROMO 4 (21 sec)
A recovery team attempts to track down a hijacked food delivery bike on the streets of Johannesburg.

VO: Sometimes the tracking team wins.

metadata.Summary: Food service delivery drivers, mostly belonging to Uber Eats and Mr DFood, have what some may consider an easy task - delivering mouth-watering food to thousands of homes daily. But, behind the helmet are stories of men and women who tell stories of daily struggles in what they see as a brutal industry. From app exploitation to daily muggings and hijackings, the relationship with motorists on the road, and the stories of those who are sitting home for months nursing injuries. The story follows 3 drivers. The story ends with a sting operation in Joburg alongside a tracking and recovery company. Our cameras will follow the company as they chase the thief trying to recover another bike.
metadata.Reason for graphics: To highlight the growth of the online food delivery industry.
